title: GPU runtime profiling: TensorRT-LLM/vLLM & CUDA graphs deep dive - Cascade AI
customer_attendees: Priya Shah - Head of ML Infra
summary: Deep technical session focused on GPU runtime profiling for large models. We compared kernel selection strategies between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM, discussed CUDA graph warmup behavior and KV-cache impacts, and walked through batching and quantization trade-offs for a 4k seq use case. Action items include sample prompt traces and a follow-up pilot run in Cascade's VPC.
next_steps: Redwood to share kernel selection benchmark spreadsheet and raw profiling traces (Liam) - due 2026-02-02
Cascade AI to provide representative prompt set, p50/p95/p99 latency targets and sample trace logs (Ethan) - due 2026-01-30
Schedule follow-up pilot run in Cascade VPC with TensorRT-LLM and vLLM variants - target week of 2026-02-09
action_items: Maya Chen - send follow-up email with links + benchmark sheet - due 2026-01-27
Liam O'Neill - export CUDA graph traces and kernel timeline, attach to benchmark sheet - due 2026-02-02
Ethan Moore - upload sample prompt traces and p99 latency target - due 2026-01-30
Daniel Kim - confirm VPC peering details and service account access for pilot - due 2026-02-03
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: OK everybody good afternoon thanks for joining. We\u0002re going to jump into GPU runtime profiling, kernel selection and the TensorRT-LLM/vLLM comparison. I\u0002m Maya, AE on the account, and Liam from our SE team will drive the deep dive.
[00:18] Priya Shah: Hi Maya, thanks. We\u0002re excited, been trying to nail down p99 on our 4k workflows, so curious about cudagraphs and warmup.
[00:30] Liam O'Neill: Great, yeah my plan -- quick context then profiling findings, then Q&A and next steps. Ethan, Daniel, feel free to interrupt.
[00:45] Ethan Moore: Sounds good. Quick context: running mix of instruction-following and retrieval-augmented prompts, mostly 4k tokens with avg 600-1200 generation tokens. Using A100s today, Kubernetes on-prem with our VPC.
[01:05] Liam O'Neill: Perfect. So first slide -- kernel selection: we talked about two strategies. One is TensorRT-LLM which compiles op-specific kernels and fuses matmuls; other approach is vLLM which uses dynamic kernel paths optimized for small-batch, low-latency. In practice we saw TRT-LLM better for steady high-throughput, vLLM wins at low-p99 for tiny batch sizes.
[01:35] Priya Shah: When you say "wins", do you mean end-to-end latency or token throughput?
[01:40] Liam O'Neill: End-to-end p50/p95/p99 mostly. Example from our benchmark: 8k sequence throughput on a single A100, TensorRT-LLM had 1.8x higher tokens/sec at batch sizes >8, but vLLM had 20-30% lower p99 at batch sizes 1-2. Note: these numbers are for the specific model topology we tested, YMMV.
[02:10] [02:15] Ethan Moore: Got it, model was a Llama-variant? Not exact name?
[02:20] Liam O'Neill: Yeah we tested on a 13B llama-derivative and a curated 34B. Also we tried quantized int8 and 4-bit.
[02:28] Daniel Kim: How stable are the CUDA graphs warmups? We saw jitter on first few requests after scale-up.
[02:34] Liam O'Neill: Great question. CUDA graphs give a huge perf up after warmup but there\u0002s a warmup tax. We typically saw 20-300ms warmup on first graph instantiation depending on seq len and KV-cache size. Important to pre-warm graphs during scale-up or use a background warmup traffic to mitigate.
[02:55] Maya Chen: Note, we sometimes saw the transcription say "cudagraphs" as one word -- I mean CUDA graphs.
[03:05] Priya Shah: (laughing) noted.
[03:12] [03:15] Liam O'Neill: Also kernel selection interacts with KV cache: vLLM keeps KV cache memory-resident with efficient layering, which helps when you have many short-turn chats. TensorRT-LLM's fused kernels benefit from larger contiguous memory layouts, better for long seq generation once kv cache is mature.
[03:40] Ethan Moore: So in our use case, we have lots of conversational context with retrieval augmentation; typical convo lengths 2-5 turns, so KV cache reuse is high. Sounds like vLLM approach might reduce p99 then?
[03:54] Liam O'Neill: Potentially yes. But if you plan to batch lots of inference requests from a webhook, TensorRT-LLM\u0002s higher throughput at larger batch sizes could lower cost. It's a trade: latency-sensitive vs cost-throughput sensitive.
[04:12] Priya Shah: Can you quantify cost delta? We need *per-token* cost estimates.
[04:19] Maya Chen: We\u0002ll share a cost-vs-latency spreadsheet; ballpark from our benchmarks: for the 13B model quantized to int8, TensorRT-LLM delivered ~30% lower GPU-hours for heavy batch workloads compared to baseline vLLM, but vLLM delivered better p99 for small batches, so your cost per request can be higher if you're doing single-shot low-latency.
[04:46] [05:00] Ethan Moore: About quantization: we\u0002ve seen hallucination increase after aggressive 4-bit quant, any notes?
[05:06] Liam O'Neill: Right, quantization is model-sensitive. For some families 4-bit QLoRA-like approaches maintain quality, others degrade. We recommend running a small eval set (we can do that) and monitoring quality regressions. Redwood Optimize suggests quantization profiles per-workload.
[05:28] Daniel Kim: On the VPC side, what are the steps to run a pilot on-prem? We are air-gapped on some clusters.
[05:35] Maya Chen: For Private deployment we provide a customer-managed control plane; for air-gapped we ship an on-prem package and documented install. For a pilot we need a service account, a peered VPC or secure ingress, and an access window -- Liam will coordinate.
[05:55] [06:00] Liam O'Neill: Back to profiling: we shared kernel-level timelines in the benchmark sheet. Key metrics: kernel occupancy, SM utilization, memcopy times, and kernel launch overhead. For TRT-LLM you\u0002ll see fewer kernel launches but longer fused kernels; for vLLM you see many smaller kernels but lower per-kernel latency.
[06:28] Priya Shah: Any best practices for batching? We have bursty traffic.
[06:34] Liam O'Neill: Dynamic batching with a short delay (5-15ms) often helps, but increases p50 a little. For latency SLOs under 200ms we keep delays near 5ms and use cache priming to reduce first-token latency. Also consider prefix caching for RAG scenarios where retrieved context repeats.
[06:56] [07:00] Ethan Moore: We use a hybrid: synchronous webhooks for interactive UI, and async queued for bulk tasks. Which runtime is better for hybrid?
[07:08] Liam O'Neill: Hybrid works: vLLM for interactive low-latency and TRT-LLM for queued bulk inference. Redwood routing can split traffic by route and SLO. You can set policy to send low-latency routes to vLLM variant and bulk routes to TRT-LLM.
[07:28] Priya Shah: Are there any gotchas with KV cache memory pressure on 80GB vs 40GB GPUs?
[07:35] Liam O'Neill: Yes memory-sizes matter. On 40GB you\u0002ll need tighter batching and quantization to fit bigger models or larger KV caches. On 80GB you can keep more offloaded states resident which helps throughput. We sometimes recommend model sharding across multiple GPUs for >70B models.
[07:58] [08:15] Maya Chen: Quick note, we\u0002ve seen subtle perf differences with cudagraph capture modes. There\u0002s capture-once vs capture-with-parameters; some runtimes capture with placeholders which reduces warmup. Liam can attach the exact traces.
[08:35] Liam O'Neill: Yes I\u0002ll attach raw cudagraph traces. We recorded first-10-request latencies and after-warmup steady-state. Example: first request 420ms, steady-state token latency 12ms, for a given setup. Numbers vary with seq length.
[08:55] Ethan Moore: Would you recommend we use pre-warm scripts during autoscale? We saw cold starts during spike.
[09:02] Liam O'Neill: Absolutely, pre-warm is key. Also consider warming specific KV cache states for RAG hot prefixes. Redwood's autoscaler can run warmup hooks.
[09:18] [09:30] Priya Shah: About kernel-level instrumentation, what tools did you use? Nsight? cuprof?
[09:35] Liam O'Neill: We used Nsight Systems for timelines and cuprof/cupti for kernel breakdowns. Also custom NVTX annotations in the runtime to map high-level ops to kernels. There can be mismatch in naming; sometimes model frameworks report different op names.
[09:55] Daniel Kim: Any differences observed between driver versions or CUDA versions?
[10:00] Liam O'Neill: Yes, CUDA 12.x vs 11.x had different kernel fusion heuristics depending on cuBLAS/cuDNN versions. We always recommend consistent driver stack and testing across the exact stack you run in prod.
[10:18] [10:30] Maya Chen: Quick demo time -- Liam are you switching to the profiling window?
[10:32] Liam O'Neill: Yep I'll share. (background screen share noises) On timeline here you can see kernel launches at ms granularity. Highlighting the fused GEMM kernels in TRT-LLM take longer but fewer launches. Over to slide that shows quantization impact.
[11:00] [11:15] Liam O'Neill: Note also how memory copies show up during KV eviction. If cache eviction is frequent you see spikes. That's why prefix caching is useful to keep hot KV entries resident.
[11:35] Ethan Moore: Is there tooling to visualize cache hits?
[11:40] Liam O'Neill: Yes our runtime exposes counters for KV hits/misses and TTLs; Redwood Console can plot these per-route. We can add a dashboard for your pilot.
[11:52] [12:00] Priya Shah: On the quantization front, you mentioned per-layer fallback for critical layers?
[12:06] Liam O'Neill: Exactly, selective quantization where you keep the attention projections in higher precision often preserves quality while getting memory wins elsewhere. We recommend layer-wise sensitivity analysis.
[12:22] [12:30] Daniel Kim: Any tips for reducing launch overhead on vLLM?
[12:35] Liam O'Neill: Keep kernels larger where possible and use batch aggregation for batched paths. Also reduce Python-level overhead by using JITed endpoints or compiled runtime. vLLM is improving here but fused kernels still help.
[12:52] [13:00] Maya Chen: We\u0002re about halfway -- open to questions.
[13:05] Priya Shah: Can you summarize pilot plan?
[13:08] Maya Chen: Sure: 1) Cascade provides prompt set and trace logs; 2) Redwood runs bench in Cascade VPC with TRT-LLM and vLLM variants, with quant profiles int8/4-bit; 3) Redwood shares raw traces and a cost-latency recommendation; 4) decide rollout.
[13:28] Ethan Moore: For the sample traces, what format do you want?
[13:32] Liam O'Neill: Prefer simple JSONL with request_id, prompt_len, gen_len, timestamp, route, and raw latency; include sequence of tokens if possible. We can also accept Prometheus histogram dumps.
[13:48] [14:00] Priya Shah: Security questions: on-prem package, is KMS/HSM supported?
[14:05] Maya Chen: Yes, Private supports customer KMS integration and HSM for key wrapping. We also provide audit logs and SAML SSO integration. More details in the security brief link I shared.
[14:24] Daniel Kim: Any compliance or SOC2 caveats?
[14:28] Maya Chen: Redwood is SOC2 Type II compliant; private deployments include supplemental attestation for on-prem when requested.
[14:40] [14:45] Ethan Moore: Back to perf -- you mentioned trace with kernel names being slightly different, is that what you described as transcription issues?
[14:52] Liam O'Neill: (laugh) yes, runtime names and trace labels sometimes abbreviated; we'll normalize in the sheet.
[15:05] [15:15] Priya Shah: For the pilot, what success metrics should we set?
[15:19] Maya Chen: Recommend 3 metrics: p99 latency under your target (e.g., <300ms), cost per 1M tokens vs baseline, and quality regression under 1% on your eval set. We'll put these in the pilot doc.
[15:35] Ethan Moore: If we see quality regressions after quant, can you do mixed-precision fallback?
[15:40] Liam O'Neill: Yes, runtime supports per-layer precision and fallback to FP16 for critical ops. Also automatic rollback in rollout policies if quality drop detected.
[15:55] [16:00] Daniel Kim: Network egress concerns: if we run in our VPC, will Redwood collect logs?
[16:05] Maya Chen: For Private, control plane can be customer-hosted; minimal telemetry shipped back unless you opt-in. We can set retention policies and anonymize traces.
[16:20] [16:30] Liam O'Neill: Quick async note: batching aggressiveness settings in Redwood can be tuned per-route in the console; we can pre-configure for pilot.
[16:45] Priya Shah: Are there any recommended GPU types aside from A100?
[16:50] Liam O'Neill: A100 and H100 are our go-tos. H100 shows perf gains on some fused kernels but requires updated CUDA stacks. For cost-sensitive smaller setups, 80GB A100 still excellent.
[17:10] [17:30] Ethan Moore: Can Redwood run a side-by-side of TRT-LLM and vLLM on same hardware to compare?
[17:36] Liam O'Neill: Yes that's the plan for the pilot \n\u0014 same infra, side-by-side traces so you can see delta.
[17:46] [18:00] Maya Chen: Any other questions?
[18:05] Priya Shah: One last one: does TensorRT-LLM support dynamic sequence lengths well? We have variable prompt sizes.
[18:12] Liam O'Neill: TensorRT-LLM prefers some shape stability for maximal fusion; it can handle dynamic seq but may need multiple specialized graphs for different length buckets. That's why CUDA graphs capture per-shape sequences helps.
[18:30] [18:45] Ethan Moore: Timing wise, how long does a pilot take?
[18:50] Maya Chen: Typical pilot 2-4 weeks: initial benching week 1, iteration week 2, optional second-run week 3. Depends on access and prompt set.
[19:05] Daniel Kim: Ok that\u0002s reasonable.
[19:10] [19:30] Liam O'Neill: Wrapping up, I\u0002ll note the four key recommendations: pre-warm cudagraphs, use vLLM variant for ultra-low p99 for single-shot, use TRT-LLM for high throughput bulk, and run layer-wise quant sensitivity tests.
[19:50] Maya Chen: Great, let\u0002s recap next steps and owners.
[20:00] [20:15] Priya Shah: Thanks everyone.
[20:20] Maya Chen: Thanks, we'll follow up with the benchmark sheet and ask for sample traces.
[20:30] [20:45] (meeting ends)

Notes: transcript contains occasional transcription artifacts and name mis-attributions in auto captions. Raw zoom audio attached in follow-up email.
